decisions.wording: Three corrections. The sentence saying narrative reviews describe the deficits as larger and more consistent is replaced: more consistent is the opposite of what both reviews say (AI reader 32, checked at Parrott 2011 p. 1365 and Parrott 2013 p. 8), and they report larger pooled differences while describing marked variation. Murphy's count is for computation span within the nine updating studies, not for updating as a whole (AI reader 31, checked at p. 161), and the review's scope (executive and visuospatial tasks) is now named, so it no longer stands behind the word memory in general. Two commas added so that the critically low confidence ratings do not read as verbs.
decisions.status: mixed, unchanged: inconsistent findings across tasks and studies with 94 to 96% heterogeneity and no adequate explanation.
decisions.grade: very low, unchanged in certainty; indirectness 0 -> 1 level. METHODS §6.3 says a claim seen only through reviews is downgraded for indirectness as second-hand, and every anchor here is a review's account of studies not read; the editor applied exactly that rule to cl_mdma_sert_binding. The claim was already at the floor, so the certainty does not move.
decisions.verification: ai-anchored, unchanged: Ung and Murphy are a meta-analysis and a systematic review read in full, so the narrative-only rule of METHODS §6.3 does not bite; the narrative-review anchors keep their second-hand labelling.

for_senior_author: The indirectness downgrade reads METHODS §6.3 as covering any claim whose primary studies were not read, including one resting on systematic reviews. If the rule is meant only for narrative reviews, the domain goes back to 0 and the certainty is unchanged either way.

Not added, for want of an anchor: Murphy reports that two other updating tasks lost their difference once cannabis was controlled (pp. 167-168). It is on the card; an anchor would have to be added and checked before the claim can say it.

decisions.wording: Two denominators corrected against the source. Table 2 reports 40 scored measures from a battery of 15 tests, so four of 40 measures differed at p < .05 and two more stood at exactly p = .05 (Raven's, digits backwards). The heavier-use subgroup's two other differences (non-dominant hand p = .003, vocabulary p = .04) are now named, so the statement matches the anchors and the GRADE reasoning.
decisions.table_4: Said exactly as the table prints it: the equivalence analysis covers the 14 measures on which the groups did not differ; the largest effect not excluded is 0.37, 0.40, 0.48, 0.49, 0.49, 0.50, 0.53, 0.54, 0.55, 0.58, 0.64, 0.66, 0.69 and 0.76. A large effect (d 0.8) is excluded on all 14; a medium effect (d 0.5) on 5, with one bound exactly 0.50 and 8 from 0.53 to 0.76. Reader 31's 6 counts the bound at 0.50; reader 32's 5 is the strict reading. The claim now gives the figures rather than a single count, and the anchors carry them.
decisions.status: single study, unchanged: the two commentaries are opposed readings of the same study, not separate evidence.
decisions.relation: does-not-detectably-change -> insufficient-evidence. METHODS §6.3 requires a no-effect claim to rest on intervals that exclude meaningful effects, not on non-significant p values. This study's own equivalence analysis leaves a medium effect in play on 9 of the 14 measures it covers (8 above 0.50 and 1 exactly at it), four whole-group measures differed and three measures differed in the heavier-use subgroup, one of them with a within-group dose relation. Both second readers proposed the change.
decisions.grade: very low, unchanged: low start, down one for risk of bias and one for imprecision. The imprecision note now carries the exact bounds, and the reasoning says why the relation is insufficient evidence.
decisions.verification: ai-anchored, unchanged: a primary study read in full, with the commentaries as qualifiers.

for_senior_author: The relation change is the one decision on this page that alters how a reader meets this study: it is no longer presented as showing no detectable change. It follows the precision rule and both second readers, but it is a judgment and is flagged for confirmation. The alternative both readers offer is to keep the old relation and narrow the outcome to the memory measures; on Table 4 even some memory bounds (verbal paired associates 0.55) leave a medium effect in play, which is why I did not take it.

Second-hand support not added: Murphy et al. (2009) describe a Hong Kong sample of 100 people who had used ecstasy and no other illicit drugs, whose Stroop performance was not significantly worse after correction (now on card sc_murphy_2009). decisions.debate: Four changes. (1) The yes side now carries Halpern et al.'s one positive finding, the strategy-application difference in the heavier-use subgroup with its within-group dose relation, which is the strongest yes-side item because it comes from the best-controlled study and supports the editors' own sentence about lifetime use. (3) The recovery and fenfluramine sentence is attributed to the commentary and qualified: the recovery is an inference from a single-time-point comparison, and the prescribing and withdrawal statements come from a legal and technical book. (4) A large effect excluded on every measure now reads on each of the 14 measures the equivalence analysis covers, with the medium-effect count; and the editors' reading no longer calls the transporter difference well attested, since every imaging figure here is second-hand and the claim is downgraded for indirectness on that ground.
